articles.title: Eating olive oil before carbs may curb blood sugar spikes: Kyoto University study reveals why
articles.summary: Imagine being told that the order in which you eat a meal could matter almost as much as what is on your plate.
articles.body: Imagine being told that the order in which you eat a meal could matter almost as much as what is on your plate. Instead of starting with rice, bread or another carbohydrate-rich food, you begin with a little fat and wait. Could that change how quickly glucose enters your bloodstream?A new study from Kyoto University suggests there may be a biological explanation for this idea. Researchers found that mice given olive oil before glucose experienced a smaller early rise in blood sugar than mice given glucose first.Their findings, published in the journal Diabeteson October 8, 2026, help explain how the timing of fat intake might influence blood sugar regulation. They do not yet establish that drinking olive oil before a meal will help people manage diabetes.What happened when researchers gave mice olive oil before glucose?The international research team, led by scientists including Daisuke Yabe of Kyoto University, wanted to understand why eating fat before carbohydrates can sometimes reduce the rise in blood glucose after a meal.To investigate, the researchers conducted experiments in mice that had fasted overnight. One group received water followed by glucose. Another received olive oil, followed by glucose 15 minutes later. A third received glucose first and olive oil 15 minutes afterwards.The scientists measured blood glucose and several hormones involved in regulating it. They also assessed how quickly the stomach emptied its contents.The results showed that giving olive oil before glucose slowed gastric emptying and reduced the early rise in blood sugar. The researchers observed similar effects in mice with type 2 diabetes and in mice whose insulin secretion was severely impaired.Why fat may slow the rise in blood sugarAfter a carbohydrate-rich meal, the digestive system breaks down digestible carbohydrates into glucose, which enters the bloodstream. The pancreas releases insulin to help the body use or store that glucose.The speed of this process varies with the meal's composition, the amount eaten and an individual's metabolism.Fat can slow the rate at which food leaves the stomach and reaches the small intestine. This process, known as gastric emptying, helps determine how quickly glucose from a meal becomes available for absorption.In the Kyoto University study, olive oil consumed before glucose delayed gastric emptying. This provided a possible explanation for the smaller early rise in blood glucose.But the researchers found that the effect was not simply a matter of slowing digestion. Several hormones appeared to be involved, pointing to a more complex response between the digestive system, pancreas and nervous system."Our findings suggest that the order in which nutrients reach the gut can engage a coordinated hormone-nerve response that changes how quickly the stomach delivers glucose to the intestine," Yabe said as per a press release available on the University's official website.Does this mean people with diabetes should eat olive oil first?Not yet. There is a crucial detail: the researchers did not test this eating strategy in people.Although the researchers observed effects in mouse models of type 2 diabetes and severe insulin deficiency, human digestion, hormone responses, meal patterns and diabetes management are more complex. Clinical studies are needed to determine whether the same mechanisms produce a meaningful benefit in people.Earlier human studies have explored meal sequencing, including eating protein and vegetables before carbohydrate-rich foods. Some have reported lower post-meal glucose excursions, but the results depend on the study design and the participants involved. Those findings do not establish that taking olive oil before carbohydrates will have the same effect.Nor does the Kyoto study show that adding extra fat to a meal is beneficial overall.People with diabetes should continue to follow their prescribed treatment and dietary advice.The Kyoto University research adds to a growing body of work examining whether meal order influences blood sugar. Its main contribution is explaining a possible mechanism: fat consumed before glucose may slow gastric emptying while engaging a coordinated response involving glucagon, GLP-1 and the vagus nerve.For now, the finding is a promising research lead, not a prescription to drink olive oil before eating rice or bread.

articles.title: Heart attack: Woman was 'dead for 10 minutes' due to 'silent' cardiac condition
articles.summary: Medics in Spain raced against time to save Sandra McCartney's life after her heart stopped beating.
articles.body:
On New Year's Eve of 2019 Sandra McCartney was clinically dead for 10 minutes.

She was 59 when she collapsed during a Christmas holiday in Spain, lost consciousness, stopped breathing and had no pulse or heartbeat after suffering a cardiac arrest.

Sandra's life was saved when medics managed to restore a normal heart rhythm during a frantic race against time when paramedics gave her "six defibrillator shocks and five shots of adrenaline".

Her life may have been turned upside down in that moment but she believes she had been living with a ticking time bomb long before that.

Sandra found out that the heart attack and cardiac arrest were triggered by a life-threatening genetic condition called "familial hypercholesterolaemia" (FH).

It causes high cholesterol and, if untreated, can lead to early heart attacks and heart disease.

A decade after a critical health service review, has there been any change?

Trust 'committed to improving facilities' with £2.5m investment in Altnagelvin ED

Dáithí Mac Gabhann returns home after heart transplant

The mother-of-four, from Londonderry, did not even know she had it.

The British Heart Foundation estimates that more than quarter of a million people in the UK have the condition, but more than two-thirds of people who have FH are never diagnosed.

However, Northern Ireland has the highest detection rate in the UK.

The experience is something that has left its mark on Sandra.

"I had three cracked ribs from the CPR (cardio-pulmonary resuscitation) and I was gone for 10 minutes before they got me back, which is terrifying to think about."

On the night she took ill, Sandra thought she had indigestion because of her "hiatus hernia" - a condition common in the over-50s, where part of the stomach moves up towards the stomach.

She alerted her husband when she began to feel an acute pain followed by a tingling sensation in her right arm.

As he tried to check if the local health centre was open in the middle of the night Sandra's pain left her and she started "drifting off".

"I was just falling into a deep sleep and he woke me, roaring at me, and shook me," she said.

She was told by a doctor she was having a major heart attack.

What is familial hypercholesterolaemia (FH)?

Familial hypercholesterolaemia (FH) is quite a common genetic condition, affecting about 1 in every 250-500 people in the population, but many people do not know they have it.

If one parent has FH, there is a 50% chance their child could have it, too.

FH can be very dangerous if left untreated, as it can lead to very high cholesterol, raising the risk of heart attacks or strokes.

Fifty per cent of men and 30% of women with untreated FH will develop coronary heart disease by the age of 55.

The good news is FH can be diagnosed quite easily and there are treatments available.

A screening service operates in Northern Ireland to provide testing for family members of people who have FH to detect as many carriers of the genes as possible.

Source: Northern Ireland Chest Heart and Stroke

She was ventilated for 11 days in hospital and her four children flew out to Spain as it was feared the worst might happen.

"I remember nothing until day four when I was brought round but a few hours later, I was ventilated again because both my lungs collapsed," she said.

"I was woken four days later but I then developed laryngeal stridor, which makes your breathing noisy and harder to do, and which is potentially life-threatening, due to being ventilated too quickly, too many times. I then had to be ventilated again. "

It was not until February that she was allowed to fly home.

Even then she had to use a wheelchair, as she had experienced so much muscle wastage over her time in hospital.

She said it was a "horrendous," not just for her but for her husband and children.

"Never in a million years did I think something like this could happen to me.

"I was fit, healthy, ate really well, I had no worries about my health."

When she returned home she had more problems.

"I wasn't home long when I passed out one day and had to be admitted to Altnagelvin Hospital for a week.

"The pandemic started soon after I was discharged so unfortunately, I didn't get any cardiac rehab which would have been so beneficial to my recovery."

She has also suffered from PTSD (post-traumatic stress disorder) and has an ICD (implantable cardioverter defibrillator) fitted which is a small electrical device because I'm at high risk of having another cardiac arrest."

Sandra's heart attack and cardiac arrest continue to affect her life to this day and there are still days when she can "do very little".

Even "something as simple as throwing a duvet on the bed", can leave her breathless.

She has never been able to return to work, though she volunteers with NI Chest Heart and Stroke and enjoys sewing.

But she is upbeat and grateful to be alive.

"Not many people survive what my body put me through."

All four of her children have tested clear for high blood pressure.

The Belfast Health Trust operates a screening service for what it calls a "silent condition".

"When someone is diagnosed with FH, their relatives are contacted and offered testing by a team of specialist nurses who cover all of Northern Ireland," a spokesperson said.

"Thanks to this programme, Northern Ireland has the highest rate of identification of FH in the UK and one of the highest rates of diagnosed cases in the world."

The trust said that once people are diagnosed and established on long-term treatment with standard cholesterol-lowering medications, they do not generally need further intervention beyond "periodic cholesterol checks".

A cardiac arrest happens when an electrical malfunction stops the heart from beating and circulating blood to the brain and vital organs - often causing permanent brain damage within minutes and sudden death.

Heart attack and cardiac arrest - the differences

A heart attack is not the same as a cardiac arrest.

A heart attack is when one of the coronary arteries becomes blocked. The heart muscle is robbed of its vital blood supply and, if left untreated, will begin to die because it is not getting enough oxygen.

A cardiac arrest is when a person's heart stops pumping blood around their body and they stop breathing normally.

Many cardiac arrests in adults happen because of a heart attack.
